title: Amma and the Egg of the World
source_ref: Dogon cosmology as published by Marcel Griaule and Germaine Dieterlen (Dieu d'eau, 1948; Le Renard pâle, 1965); a contested account
paragraphs: Amma is the creator in Dogon accounts, a sky god who existed before the world. One influential description, published by Marcel Griaule and Germaine Dieterlen, says that Amma shaped a cosmic egg and set within it the seeds of all things. That description is a synthesis, not a simple record of a single shared Dogon religion.

In the Griaule-Dieterlen account, the egg contained pairs of twins, the Nommo, who were meant to bring order and fertility. Amma created the earth and the waters for them. One of the first pair, Ogo, acted before his time and broke the intended pairing. That premature act is one explanation for disorder in the world.

Amma then ordered the world: sky above, earth below, water in its channels, and the seasons in their turn. The other twins, the Nommo, became mediators between heaven and earth, carrying rain and the words of creation. The account gives Amma a plan, but it also shows that the plan was disturbed from the beginning.

This is one contested account, not the whole of Dogon thought. Later scholars, especially Walter van Beek, found little evidence that the elaborate system was shared across Dogon communities. Many Dogon today are Muslim or Christian and keep ancestral practices in varied ways. The story is retold here as published cosmology, with that disagreement openly acknowledged.
notes: The cosmic egg, the paired Nommo and the detailed sequence of creation come mainly from the Griaule-Dieterlen corpus, which later fieldwork has strongly questioned. Dogon communities hold varied religious ideas, and the account should not be taken as a uniform 'Dogon religion'.

title: The Nommo and the Ark
source_ref: Griaule and Dieterlen's published Dogon corpus, with Dogon oral tradition; some related knowledge is restricted
paragraphs: The Nommo are the ancestral twins of Dogon cosmology. In the published Griaule-Dieterlen account, Amma made them as amphibious beings, at home in water and air, and they served as intermediaries between the creator and the world. One of them was sacrificed so that creation could be restored. Dogon oral tradition remembers the Nommo in many ways.

The Nommo descended to earth in an ark, a vessel that carried the first seeds, animals and tools. In some versions the ark is a basket or a granary; in others it is a ship. It came down at a place in the cliff country, and the ancestors stepped out to found the villages and teach the arts of life.

The ark brought water, the condition of all fertility, and it brought speech, the gift that makes community possible. The Nommo taught people to farm, to weave, to work iron and to speak with one another. Rain is still read as a sign of their continuing presence, and the first ancestors are honoured in rites that vary from village to village.

Some of this knowledge is restricted. Certain myths, names and rites belong to initiation and are not told to outsiders, and this retelling makes no claim to reveal them. It stays with the published outline and with what Dogon tellers have chosen to share. Details differ between villages, families and recorders, and the Griaule-Dieterlen synthesis remains disputed.
notes: The ark, the sacrifice of a Nommo and the descent to a specific place are presented differently across Dogon tellings and are central to the contested Griaule-Dieterlen synthesis. Some associated ritual knowledge is restricted to initiated elders and is deliberately not described here.

title: Sunjata's Childhood
source_ref: Mande epic of Sunjata as performed by jeliw (griots); Djibril Tamsir Niane, Sundiata: An Epic of Old Mali (1960)
paragraphs: Sogolon was a woman of unusual origin, remembered as the buffalo woman. She married Maghan Kon Fatta, king of the Mande, and became pregnant with a child who was long in coming. The pregnancy was difficult, and the court watched with impatience. In the epic, her son's destiny is felt before he is born, but the signs are not yet clear.

The child was named Sunjata. For years he did not walk. He crawled and dragged himself, and the other children laughed. His mother endured the shame in silence. Sassouma Bérété, the king's senior wife, mocked Sogolon and her son who could not walk, and pressed the claim of her own child, Dankaran Touman, to the throne.

One day Sassouma sent Sogolon to gather baobab leaves, a task meant to humiliate her. Sunjata asked his mother for an iron rod. He pulled himself upright, took a step, then another, and walked. Then he uprooted a baobab tree and carried it to her. The court that had laughed now fell silent, and fear replaced mockery.

The epic does not agree on every detail: the number of years Sunjata could not walk, the exact insult and the order of events differ between performances. Djibril Tamsir Niane's widely read version, based on a griot's telling, is a literary retelling rather than a transcript. The story is carried by jeliw, hereditary griots, and it changes in the telling.
notes: Epic performances vary in the length of Sogolon's pregnancy, the number of years Sunjata cannot walk, the insult that provokes him and the order of the baobab episode. Niane's book is a literary shaping of one griot's narrative, not a fixed or verbatim text, and the epic is still performed.

title: Sunjata and Soumaoro
source_ref: Mande epic of Sunjata (Niane 1960; David C. Conrad 2004) and the limited external historical record
paragraphs: Soumaoro Kanté, king of Sosso, ruled through fear and was said to command powers that ordinary weapons could not touch. The Mande clans, tired of his raids, gathered around Sunjata. The epic brings together old rivals and makes them allies: the Keita, the Traoré, the Kamara and others. Their union is the political heart of the story.

Two figures matter at court. Balla Fasséké is Sunjata's griot, the keeper of names and memory. Fakoli is Soumaoro's nephew, a warrior of great strength, who turns against his uncle after a deep humiliation. In Niane's telling, Soumaoro takes Fakoli's wife, and Fakoli's anger opens a way for the alliance. Griots tell the cause differently.

The armies met at Kirina. Soumaoro's protective power gave him an advantage, but Balla Fasséké learned that this power had a limit, and Sunjata struck him with an arrow tipped with a white rooster's spur. The king of Sosso fled and vanished, and the Mande alliance held the field. The epic turns this victory into the founding of Mali.

Historians accept that a Mali Empire rose in the thirteenth century, and the epic remembers Kirina as its founding battle, but the written record is thin and gives few details. The epic is not a chronicle: it is a performed account of origins, shaped by the families who keep it. Its truth is remembered and contested, not documentary.
notes: The battle is traditionally dated to about 1235, but the main narrative is the epic itself, which exists in many performance variants. Soumaoro's magical protection, the white rooster's spur and Fakoli's motive differ between tellings. The epic is not a chronicle, and the external written evidence for these events is limited.

title: The Pale Fox and Divination
source_ref: Dogon accounts of Ogo (Yurugu) in Griaule and Dieterlen, with later ethnographic critique
paragraphs: Ogo, also called Yurugu, is the pale fox of Dogon accounts. In the Griaule-Dieterlen system he is a first being who acted before his time, seizing what was not yet his and breaking the intended pairing of creation. His impatience brings disorder, drought and sterility into the world. The story explains why the world is not perfectly ordered.

Ogo is not simply a villain. He is associated with the bush, with hunger and with the knowledge that comes from looking at what went wrong. In the published account, his movements leave signs, and those signs can be read. That is the mythic basis for divination, though practice and myth do not always match neatly.

In fox divination, a diviner marks a grid of squares in the sand and places questions or symbols in them. Overnight, a fox walks across the grid. At dawn the diviner reads the tracks, matching the prints to the squares and to the client's question. The practice is still used, and it is a craft of interpretation rather than a fixed codebook.

Ogo's identification with the fox, and the elaborate mythology around him, come largely from the Griaule-Dieterlen corpus, which later scholars have questioned. Diviners themselves describe their work in practical terms, and not every Dogon community tells the same story. The retelling keeps the myth and the practice distinct, and marks both as uncertain.
notes: The identification of Ogo with the pale fox and the cosmic role given to him are strongest in the Griaule-Dieterlen corpus and are not uniformly attested. Fox divination is a living practice with local variation, and its rules are learned through apprenticeship; this retelling does not claim to give a complete or authoritative account.

title: Faro and the Waters
source_ref: Dogon accounts of Faro in Griaule and Dieterlen and later recordings, with Mande and Bambara parallels; regional variants
paragraphs: Faro is a water spirit and lawgiver honoured in Mande, Bambara and Dogon traditions. In the Griaule-Dieterlen version, he is linked with the Nommo, and after Ogo's rebellion he is the power that restores order. Water is his element and his instrument: rain, rivers and the moisture that makes the fields fertile. Without him, the world would remain dry and disordered.

Faro separates the waters and sets them in their places. He gives the world its seasons, the rains that come and go, and the rhythm of planting and harvest. He also gives speech, the ordered word that allows people to live together. In this account, law and fertility are two sides of the same gift.

The restoration is not a single act. Faro teaches, judges and renews, and the rites that honour him are tied to the agricultural year. The great Sigui cycle, held about once every sixty years, belongs to a wider world of Dogon renewal, though its myths are distinct and much of its detail is restricted. Rain rituals and water shrines remain important in Dogon country.

Faro's position varies. Some tellings give him a larger role, as a rain spirit or a creator figure; others make him a subordinate of Amma or give him a twin or counterpart. The coherent Griaule-Dieterlen portrait is one interpretation, contested by later fieldwork. This retelling keeps to the published outline, notes the variants, and does not claim access to restricted teaching.
notes: Faro's rank and role vary between accounts and regions: he is sometimes a Nommo, sometimes a separate water spirit, and Mande and Bambara tellings differ from the Dogon material. The systematised portrait comes from the contested Griaule-Dieterlen corpus, while rain, water and renewal rites remain living practices with restricted elements.
